claims.text: Nickel-based superalloy components such as turbine-disk materials can possess heterogeneous microstructures and be susceptible to hot cracking during fusion-welding repair.
Localized friction stir processing generates a refined near-surface microstructure.
Localized friction stir processing homogenizes the near-surface microstructure and diminishes microsegregation.
The refined and homogenized surface produced by FSP significantly delays hot cracking relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP improves surface mechanical properties relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
FSP can be performed using a tungsten-based non-consumable tool.
Optimized rotation speed, traverse speed, and plunge depth are required for the proposed localized FSP treatment.
In-situ monitoring ensures consistent engagement of the near-surface region.
FSP is a solid-state process that can be conducted below the melting temperature.
The proposed treatment is confined to a shallow near-surface layer a few millimeters deep.
FSP imposes severe plastic deformation and localized frictional heating in the near-surface zone.
FSP-induced deformation and heating cause dynamic recrystallization in the near-surface zone.
The FSP-induced microstructural transformation eliminates fusion-induced defects and inhomogeneities.
Removing microstructural heterogeneities mitigates sites that initiate hot cracking.
The FSP-treated surface will have greater hardness than both fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The FSP-treated surface will have greater resistance to microcrack initiation than both fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The FSP-treated surface will perform better in aggressive high-temperature service environments than fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
